---
title: "Read Agent-Written Pipelines"
---

::: {.ao-story}
The rails your companion laid look sound from a distance, but one points at a private road and another melts the cargo it carries. Nothing it said gave warning. Reading the rails yourself is how you find the flaws. Learn the four that turn up most.
:::

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will spot the common mistakes in agent-written pipeline rules by reading them.
- **Before you start:** [Dry Run First](dry-run-first.html).
- **Time:** about 10 minutes.
:::

You need to read pipeline code before you trust it. A **rule** is one step of a Snakemake pipeline: it names the inputs, outputs and command. An agent can write rules that run and still produce the wrong result, so reading them is part of the check. Pipelines fail quietly in a few recurring ways. When you review a rule, ask where each input comes from, where each output goes, and what would change if you re-ran it.

Here is a Snakemake rule with the first two mistakes:

```python
rule count_lines:
    input: "/home/alice/data/sample1.fastq"
    shell: "wc -l {input} > counts.txt"
```

- The input is a **hard-coded path** to one person's home folder and one sample.
- The rule has no `output:` line, so Snakemake does not know that `counts.txt` is made. The file is an **undeclared output**, so Snakemake cannot track it or build the next step from it.

Four common mistakes. The first two are in the rule above:

- **Hard-coded path:** a path to someone's home directory or to one sample.
- **Undeclared output:** the workflow manager (the tool that runs the steps, such as Snakemake or Nextflow) cannot tell what a step made.
- **Unpinned tool version** (no fixed version stated): results change when the environment does.
- **Overwritten inputs:** a step changes its input in place, so there is no way back.

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Distribution and Reproducibility](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/en/stable/snakefiles/deployment.html): Snakemake, docs. Why read: it covers per-rule conda environments, containers and pinning, the answer to unpinned tools.
- [Conda environments](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/conda): Seqera (Nextflow), docs. Why read: it shows pinning by version and lock files that record every package.
- [Containers](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/container): Seqera (Nextflow), docs. Why read: it shows setting a container per process; it gives no rule on tags or digests, so pin by your own policy.
- [Caching and resuming](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/cache-and-resume): Seqera (Nextflow), docs. Why read: it lists what goes into a task hash, including the stub-run flag, and why a process that edits its inputs cannot resume.
:::
